title: Ulyana and the Machine
premise: Vesper Thornbury, a xenolinguist whose mind has drifted so far into alien grammar that she no longer dreams in human languages, works the long haul between colonies that have gone silent. When a derelict ship returns from deep space carrying its crew aged backward into childhood, Vesper discovers the anomaly is tied to an inheritance her estranged mother left buried in the ship's translation core: a signal that can wake only half of humanity's frozen sleepers before the network fails. Torn between the found family of her crew and the children who carry her mother's choices, Vesper must decode which half lives—and in choosing, finally claim a language, and a family, of her own.
about_author: Cyrus Marchetti is the pen name of a former shipping-route logistics analyst who spent eleven years writing dispatches from orbital freight terminals. Their fiction explores the quiet mathematics of people who belong to schedules more than places.

chapters.title: The Long Route
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Aboard the freighter Meridian, Vesper translates a dying colony's last transmission and realizes she dreamed last night in a language with no human speakers. Her crew—engineer Dov, medic Sefa, and the ship AI called Auntie—tease her gently over dinner. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence; she is loved but doesn't feel it.

chapters.title: Return of the Unaged
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The Meridian intercepts the Halcyon, a deep-space vessel missing for forty years, crewed now by adults turned into children. Vesper is the only one who can read the ship's corrupted logs. One child, Ilya, speaks to her in perfect Old Common—a dead language. Emotional beat: dread and recognition; something here knows her name.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Voice
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV, fragmented and childlike. The boy remembers being sixty years old and hearing a woman named Maren Thornbury record a message 'for whoever wakes up small.' He carries fragments of it like stones in his pockets. Emotional beat: inherited grief; the child holds an adult's unfinished business he cannot understand.

chapters.title: Cryosleep Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Dov's POV. The engineer decodes the Halcyon's power signature: the cryo-network sustaining two million sleepers across the colonies will fail within months, and the Halcyon's core holds the only override—but it can restore just half. Dov hides the math from Vesper, protecting her. Emotional beat: love expressed as concealment, and its cost.

chapters.title: Grammar of the Deep
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Studying the core, Vesper recognizes the signal structure: it isn't human engineering at all but a language—one her drifting mind already half-speaks. Her mother didn't build the machine; she negotiated with whatever did. Emotional beat: vertigo and awe as Vesper's 'brokenness' reveals itself as fluency.

chapters.title: What the Children Remember
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. The unaged crew members begin sharing memories that don't match their logs—memories of a future that hasn't happened, including one of Vesper standing at the core making a choice. Sefa must decide whether to tell her. Emotional beat: the terror of foreknowledge and tenderness toward people who are both old and new.

chapters.title: Thornbury Inheritance
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Following coordinates in Maren's final message, Vesper finds her mother's hidden habitat: recordings, apologies, and proof that Maren traded decades of contact with her daughter for the negotiation that kept humanity's sleepers alive this long. Emotional beat: rage curdling into mourning; Vesper stops waiting for an apology that was always encoded in the work itself.

chapters.title: Half of Everyone
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. The crew argues over the selection criteria while the network's failure accelerates; colonies begin going dark. Ilya tells Vesper the machine doesn't want a list—it wants someone who can speak its grammar honestly, and it will know if she lies. Emotional beat: moral crisis; every criterion for choosing is a way of deciding who deserves to exist.

chapters.title: The Waking Word
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, climax. At the core, Vesper refuses both preset lists and instead translates herself—offering her own divided identity, human and otherwise, as the key. The machine accepts a third option she finds in the grammar: staggered waking, slower, costlier, but whole. She dreams, for the first time, in two languages at once. Emotional beat: self-acceptance as the hinge of salvation.

chapters.title: Dreaming in Common
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV, resolution. Months later, the first revived sleepers step onto a green colony world alongside the unaged children. Ilya, aging forward again, watches Vesper teach a classroom of returnees and strangers the same new words. Auntie plays a lullaby Maren recorded long ago. Emotional beat: belonging not as inheritance received but as family built—and passed on.
